parts.problem_md:
The scientist investigates the effect of three different fertilisers on the crop yield of maize plants.

Table 3.1 shows the results of the investigation.

**Table 3.1**

| fertiliser used | formula for ion | days until harvest | crop yield / thousand kg per Ha |
|---|---|---|---|
| nitrate | .......... | 94 | 31 |
| phosphate | .......... | 98 | 28 |
| potassium | K⁺ | 95 | 25 |
| control |   | 96 | 18 |

State two control variables in this investigation.
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Any **two** from:
> 
> - The mass or concentration of fertiliser
> - The number of maize plants
> - The area of the field
> - The planting density
> - The volume of water given
> - The type, variety or age of the maize seeds or plants
> 
> **[2 marks]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> - Be precise about quantities. Write 'volume of water' or 'mass of fertiliser', not 'amount'.

The scientist investigates the effect of three different fertilisers on the crop yield of maize plants.

Table 3.1 shows the results of the investigation.

**Table 3.1**

| fertiliser used | formula for ion | days until harvest | crop yield / thousand kg per Ha |
|---|---|---|---|
| nitrate | .......... | 94 | 31 |
| phosphate | .......... | 98 | 28 |
| potassium | K⁺ | 95 | 25 |
| control |   | 96 | 18 |

Give one conclusion about the effect of fertilisers on the crop yield of maize.

Justify your conclusion.
parts.solution_md:
Conclusion: fertilisers increase the crop yield of maize  **[1 mark]**.

Justification: all three fertilisers gave a higher yield (25 to 31 thousand kg per hectare) than the control (18 thousand kg per hectare)  **[1 mark]**.

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **Mark allocation**
> 
> - **One mark** for a valid conclusion and **one mark** for a justification that matches it
> 
> **Alternative content**
> 
> The answer above is just one example of how to respond to this question. Other information that could be used includes:
> 
> - Conclusion: nitrate has the greatest effect on crop yield. Justification: nitrate gives the highest yield (31 thousand kg per hectare)
> - Any other suitable response

> **[exam-tip]**
> - A conclusion should sum up all the results, not just one fertiliser, unless you are comparing the fertilisers with each other.

parts.problem_md:
The scientist investigates the effect of three different fertilisers on the crop yield of maize plants.

Table 3.1 shows the results of the investigation.

**Table 3.1**

| fertiliser used | formula for ion | days until harvest | crop yield / thousand kg per Ha |
|---|---|---|---|
| nitrate | .......... | 94 | 31 |
| phosphate | .......... | 98 | 28 |
| potassium | K⁺ | 95 | 25 |
| control |   | 96 | 18 |

The scientist concludes:

'Adding fertiliser to maize crops decreases the number of days until harvest.'

Explain one way the data:

supports the conclusion

does not support the conclusion
parts.solution_md:
Supports: maize with nitrate (94 days) and potassium (95 days) was ready sooner than the control (96 days)  **[1 mark]**.

Does not support: maize with phosphate took longer (98 days) than the control  **[1 mark]**.

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **Mark allocation**
> 
> - **One mark** for a valid way the data supports the conclusion
> - **One mark** for a valid way the data does not support it
> 
> **Alternative content**
> 
> The answer above is just one example of how to respond to this question. Other information that could be used includes:
> 
> - The differences from the control are only one or two days, which may not be significant
> - Any other suitable response

> **[exam-tip]**
> - Quote the figures and say how they compare with the control. Copying numbers from the table without comparing them does not score.

parts.problem_md:
The scientist also uses a systematic sampling strategy to estimate the population of giant African land snails.

Suggest benefits and limitations of using a systematic sampling strategy to estimate the population of giant African land snails in Florida.
parts.solution_md:
Benefits: the samples are spread evenly over the whole area  **[1 mark]**, and the method is simple to repeat to check the results  **[1 mark]**.

Limitation: snails that are clustered between the sampling points may be missed, so the estimate may not be representative  **[1 mark]**.

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **Mark allocation**
> 
> - **One mark** for each valid benefit or limitation, to a maximum of 3 marks
> - A maximum of **2 marks** for benefits and a maximum of **2 marks** for limitations
> 
> **Alternative content**
> 
> The answer above is just one example of how to respond to this question. Other information that could be used includes:
> 
> - Florida is a very large area, so sampling it systematically is difficult
> - Choosing the sampling interval can introduce bias
> - Any other suitable response

parts.problem_md:
A scientist wants to use a random sampling strategy to estimate the population of giant African land snails in Florida.

Describe a random sampling strategy to estimate the population of giant African land snails in Florida.

In your answer include a method to:

- select the area to sample
- collect and record your data
- estimate the population of giant African land snails in Florida.
parts.solution_md:
Put a grid over a map of Florida  **[1 mark]** and use a random number generator to choose grid squares to sample  **[1 mark]**. At each site, place a 1 m² quadrat and count the snails inside it  **[1 mark]**, recording each count in a tally table  **[1 mark]**. Repeat this for at least 50 quadrats, then multiply the mean number of snails per m² by the area of Florida  **[1 mark]**.

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **Mark allocation**
> 
> This answer is assessed using a point-marked approach.
> 
> - **One mark** for each valid point, to a maximum of 5 marks
> - You must cover all three bullet points to gain 5 marks
> 
> **Alternative content**
> 
> The answer above is just one example of how to respond to this question. Other information that could be used includes:
> 
> - Use GPS coordinates to find the sampling sites
> - Repeat the sampling on several days and use the mean
> - Any other suitable response
> 
> **Common errors**
> 
> - Describing systematic sampling, for example sampling at regular intervals, when the question asks for random sampling
> - Forgetting to repeat the sampling

> **[exam-tip]**
> - Use the three bullets as headings in your plan and give at least one point under each.
> - Do not copy the question into your answer. Start straight away with what you would do.

parts.problem_md:
In 2022, two populations of giant African land snails were found in the state of Florida, USA.

Figure 2.2 shows the location of these two populations.

![Map of Florida showing two giant African land snail populations, marked by black dots labelled 1 in the south-east and 2 on the west coast. A scale bar shows 0–75 kilometres; north, south, east and west are marked.](assets/001-map-of-florida-showing-two-giant-african-land-sn.png)

*Figure 2.2*

Give the direction of population 2 from population 1.

Figure 1.1 shows data collected at a farm in Finland.

![Dual-axis bar-and-line chart of mean monthly precipitation and temperature in Finland. Precipitation Jan–Dec is 44, 32, 36, 34, 35, 54, 79, 81, 64, 64, 60 and 52 mm; October and November temperatures are 4 and minus 1 degrees Celsius.](assets/002-dual-axis-bar-and-line-chart-of-mean-monthly-pre.png)

*Figure 1.1 -NASA's Earth Observatory*

A student uses the data in Figure 1.1 to make two conclusions:

- February is always the wettest month in Finland.
- The temperature in October is always higher than the temperature in November in Finland.

Suggest two limitations of these conclusions.

Explain these limitations.
parts.solution_md:
Limitation 1: The data come from one farm, so they may not represent the whole of Finland  **[1 mark]**.

Explanation 1: Other parts of Finland have different temperatures and precipitation, so the pattern could be different there  **[1 mark]**.

Limitation 2: The data are mean values, so they do not show what happens in each year  **[1 mark]**.

Explanation 2: Weather varies from year to year, so in some years November could be warmer than October  **[1 mark]**.

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **Mark allocation**
> 
> This answer is assessed using a point-marked approach.
> 
> - **One mark** for each limitation and **one mark** for its matching explanation, to a maximum of 4 marks
> 
> **Alternative content**
> 
> The answer above is just one example of how to respond to this question. Other information that could be used includes:
> 
> - The climate is changing, so past data may not show future patterns
> - The conclusions say 'always', which one set of data cannot prove
> - Figure 1.1 shows August, not February, as the wettest month, so the first conclusion is not supported by the data
> - Any other suitable response

> **[exam-tip]**
> - Each explanation must match its limitation. Write the explanation straight after the limitation so the examiner can see they belong together.
